anomaly_def.Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Exhaustion of physical or logical free space for data files, logs, temp areas, backups, or diagnostic outputs, leading to allocation failures and write stalls.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Hitting kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas, preventing the database from opening files, spawning workers, or attaching shared memory.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Saturation or exhaustion of listener, socket, authentication, or network bandwidth resources that blocks new client connections or slows data transfer.

When all three anomalies manifest together, symptoms overlap and amplify: connection attempts pile up while the listener’s socket queues are full and kernel file-descriptor limits are reached; existing sessions hang in client I/O or log-file-write waits because archive, redo, or temp spaces are full; background processes fail to allocate shared memory or threads, yet errors cannot be written because diagnostic log files and destinations lack space. Administrators observe surging connection timeouts, "too many open files" or "cannot allocate memory" errors, sudden inability to create new sessions, and critical write failures for data, temp, or log files. Performance degrades erratically—some transactions block on space, others on OS resource denials, while still others stall on network retransmissions—making the outage pattern appear intermittent and hard to pinpoint.

Causal chain: space exhaustion in logs or datafiles forces the database to issue additional file-open, extend, and archive operations, rapidly consuming file handles and shared memory descriptors, thereby triggering OS resource limit breaches. Once kernel limits are hit, the listener and background writers cannot open new sockets or files, which in turn causes connection queues to back up and network sockets to linger in half-open states, aggravating the network resource bottleneck. Simultaneously, clients retry failed connections, inflating the socket and process counts and accelerating OS limit exhaustion, while prolonged result streaming holds disk space and network buffers longer, further delaying log archival and space reclamation. The intertwined feedback loops among dwindling storage, depleted kernel resources, and choked connectivity quickly cascade into a full system outage that is more severe and harder to remediate than any single anomaly alone.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time after which a TCP keepalive message that has not been acknowledged by the client should be retransmitted.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP keepalive probe is not acknowledged for tcp_keepalives_interval on systems supporting TCP_KEEPINTVL or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Controls retry timing for keepalive probes used to detect unresponsive client connections.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
